statement: Five whole numbers have an odd sum and an even product. At most how many of the five numbers can be odd?

choices.misconception: I thought an even product means every number must be even, but one even number is enough.
I thought an odd sum needs exactly one odd number, but three odd numbers also make an odd sum.
I kept one number even for the product but forgot that four odd numbers add up to an even total.
I made the sum odd with five odd numbers but forgot that their product would then be odd.

hints: When is a sum of whole numbers odd?
A sum is odd exactly when it contains an odd count of odd numbers. A product is even as soon as one of the numbers is even. Combine the two facts.
The count of odd numbers must be 1, 3 or 5, and it cannot be all five.

solutions.reliable: Even numbers never change whether a sum is odd or even, and each odd number flips it. So the sum is odd exactly when there are 1, 3 or 5 odd numbers. The product is even exactly when at least one number is even, so not all five can be odd. The largest count left is 3, and it works: 1 + 3 + 5 + 2 + 4 = 15 is odd, and $1 \times 3 \times 5 \times 2 \times 4 = 120$ is even. The transferable idea: the parity of a sum depends only on how many odd numbers it has, and a product is odd only when every number in it is odd.

whyOnTest: Parity questions test two rules at once: an odd sum needs an odd count of odd numbers, and one even number makes a product even.
